pass_name: Government That Belongs to the People
governing_proposition: The people are sovereign. Government exercises delegated power. Markets organize enormous amounts of economic activity. The Constitution establishes boundaries neither political majorities nor economic power should be allowed to casually cross.
opposition_test: Design every power as though the person you trust least will eventually control it.
citizens_govern_line: Evidence informs. Experts administer. Institutions constrain. Citizens govern.
closing_argument: Constitutional Capitalism does not ask Arkansans to trust government more. Nor does it ask them to trust corporations, experts, algorithms, political parties or wealthy benefactors more. It asks us to build institutions that require less trust because power can be seen, challenged, divided, measured and ultimately returned to the people from whom it came.
landing_definition: Government should be strong enough to protect a free society, capable enough to serve it, and constrained enough that it can never legitimately claim to own it.

government_roles.q: Places public capital at risk or owns an asset.

capture_breaker_families.q: Government doesn't quietly create protected insiders.
Someone outside the decision chain can examine it.
Money and performance can be traced.

ai_power_levels.q: AI helps a human do work.
AI materially influences a decision affecting someone.
A system determines or effectively determines a consequential outcome.

misconception_boxes.title: Is this big government?
misconception_boxes.explain: Government size is a crude measure. The more important questions are: What does it do? Why? At what level? With what authority? Under what constraints? Who can challenge it?

misconception_boxes.title: Does CC distrust successful businesses?
misconception_boxes.explain: It distrusts capture. A company becoming enormously successful through innovation, competition and voluntary exchange is consistent with capitalism. Using political power to close markets, socialize private risk or secure privileged treatment is a different mechanism.

sections.heading: Give the government to the person you trust least
prose: Imagine every government power proposed in this book is placed tomorrow into the hands of the politician you trust least. Would you still grant that power?
That's the Opposition Test. People routinely evaluate government power based on who currently controls it. Constitutional design requires the opposite.
Design every power as though the person you trust least will eventually control it.

sections.heading: Government is necessary
prose: Markets require institutions. Property requires rules. Contracts require enforcement. Rights require protection. Infrastructure requires coordination. Crime requires lawful response. Disputes require adjudication. Public health and emergencies require institutions. Elections require administration.
A constitutional market society does not exist without functioning government.
Weak government is not the same thing as limited government. A government incapable of enforcing its own constitutional rules can leave power to whoever is strongest.

sections.heading: But necessary power is still power
prose: Taxation can finance legitimate government — or become extraction. Regulation can protect markets — or protect incumbents. Police power can protect people — or violate rights. Public investment can build capability — or become political patronage. Data can improve administration — or enable surveillance. AI can make government more capable — or make opaque decisions at enormous scale.
The question isn't whether government should have power. It is what power, for what purpose, under what rules, with what limits, and accountable to whom.

sections.heading: The sovereignty chain
prose: People → Constitution → Government → Administration → Public Action — then Accountability returns to the People.
Citizens delegate authority. They do not permanently surrender sovereignty.
Winning an election grants an office. It does not transfer ownership of the republic.

sections.heading: Constitutional Capitalism begins with a Constitution for a reason
prose: Capitalism describes important parts of how economic production, markets, investment and ownership work. Constitutional tells us those forces operate inside a political order with rights, boundaries and democratic legitimacy.
Without functioning markets and private capital, CC becomes something else. Without constitutional restraints, it can become state capitalism, oligarchy, crony capitalism or majoritarian domination.
The Constitution isn't a brake attached to Constitutional Capitalism. It is part of the engine.

sections.heading: Rights are floors
prose: There are some things government should not be allowed to do merely because 51% voted for it, a governor wants it, a legislature passed it, an agency finds it efficient, or an AI system recommends it.
The people are sovereign collectively while individual people retain constitutional rights.
Democracy without rights floors can become majority domination. Rights without democracy can become rule by institutions detached from the people. CC needs both.

sections.heading: Democracy is more than Election Day
prose: People → elections/direct democracy → representatives → laws → administration → budgets/contracts/services → real-world outcomes → measurement → accountability → People.
The Power Loop doesn't end when votes are counted. If citizens cannot understand what government subsequently did, democratic control becomes theoretical.

sections.heading: Comprehensible Government
prose: Government can technically disclose enormous quantities of information while remaining functionally opaque. A 900-page PDF isn't necessarily transparency. A procurement database nobody understands isn't necessarily accountability.
Citizens should be able to understand what their government decided, why it decided it, what it cost, who benefited, and what happened afterward.
That's Comprehensible Government — more demanding than merely posting documents.

sections.heading: Follow the public dollar
prose: Taxpayer / Public Revenue → appropriation → agency → program/procurement/investment → recipient/provider → output → outcome → measurement.
At each point ask: Who authorized it? How much? For what purpose? Who received it? What was promised? What happened?
That's the Public Dollar Chain — connecting Chapter 3's money logic to democratic accountability.

sections.heading: Four roles government can play
prose: Rulemaker sets legal boundaries. Provider directly provides a public function. Purchaser buys from another provider. Investor/Owner places public capital at risk or owns an asset.
These roles are not interchangeable. A government regulating an industry while owning a competitor inside it creates potential conflicts — hence the Role Conflict Test.

sections.heading: The Role Conflict Test
prose: Imagine the referee also owns one team. Even if the referee behaves perfectly, everyone has reason to question the game.
If government regulates, finances, owns, and judges the same market simultaneously, institutional conflicts can arise.
That doesn't mean government can never occupy multiple roles. It means those roles require separation, transparency and justification.

sections.heading: Solve problems at the lowest capable level
prose: Should every pothole decision be made in Little Rock? Obviously not. Should every Arkansas town independently maintain its own university research system? Probably not. Different problems operate at different scales.
Subsidiarity: Place authority as close to the people as practical, but high enough to possess the capability and legal authority necessary to solve the problem.

sections.heading: The Subsidiarity Ladder
prose: Individual/Household → Neighborhood/Community → Municipality → County/Region → State → Federal — with arrows moving both ways.
Don't automatically push everything downward. A tiny community may lack capacity for a specialized service. Regional systems may be better. Federal constitutional protections remain floors.
Local where capable and lawful; larger-scale where scale or capacity requires it; constitutional rights never depend on ZIP code.

sections.heading: Localism can fail too
prose: Local government is not inherently virtuous because it is local. A local government can be captured, corrupt, incompetent, exclusionary, or abusive — and so can state or federal government.
Constitutional Capitalism doesn't worship governmental scale. It asks: Which level can perform the function effectively while remaining closest to meaningful democratic accountability?

sections.heading: Administration matters
prose: Elections receive enormous attention. Administration receives much less. But administration determines whether licenses are issued, benefits arrive, contracts work, roads get maintained, systems function, records are accurate, and laws become reality.
A brilliant statute administered badly is still bad government.
CC requires capable bounded administration. Both words matter: Capable. Bounded.

sections.heading: The Mediocre Government Test
prose: Don't design a program assuming brilliant people administer it forever.
Would this system still function reasonably under an ordinary administration filled with ordinary people making ordinary mistakes?
If it requires genius, heroism or perfect integrity every day, the design is fragile. Government systems need clear rules, defaults, checks, appeals, audit trails, and understandable objectives.

sections.heading: Economic power becomes political power
prose: Money buys things. It can also buy access, lobbying, legal expertise, advertising, political organization, information, campaign capacity, and influence.
That doesn't make wealth evil. Political participation is a right. But concentrated economic power can become concentrated political power — then political power can reshape economic rules.
That's the beginning of the Capture Loop.

sections.heading: The Capture Loop
prose: Concentrated economic power → political influence → favorable rules/contracts/access → greater economic advantage → greater concentrated economic power — then repeat.
A company becoming rich because millions voluntarily buy a superior product is one thing. A company becoming protected from competition through political power is another.
CC wants markets producing wealth. It does not want wealth purchasing the market's rules.

sections.heading: Eight capture-breaker families
prose: Transparency. Competition. Disclosure. Recusal. Independent review. Audit. Appeal. Exit/sunset.
These aren't guarantees of virtuous leadership. They're circuit breakers — mechanisms that make capture harder and recovery possible.

sections.heading: Public Deal Ledger
prose: When public resources materially support a private deal, citizens should be able to answer: What did we contribute? What did the recipient promise? Who bears risk? Who receives upside? What happens if promises aren't met? When does the arrangement end? What actually happened?
That's a Public Deal Ledger — not a scandal database. An accountability infrastructure.

sections.heading: Pay-to-play without a speech war
prose: We should not solve political influence by simply punishing lawful political speech.
Focus on government conduct: procurement rules, disclosures, conflict rules, recusal, cooling-off structures where lawful, auditability, competitive processes.
The target is corrupting the public decision — not silencing political participation.

sections.heading: Direct democracy as a pressure-release valve
prose: Representative government can become insulated. Direct democracy can provide citizens another mechanism.
Direct democracy can correct representative failure. It cannot erase constitutional rights.
This defends citizen initiative without pretending majorities are infallible.

sections.heading: AI enters government
prose: AI can help government summarize, search, detect anomalies, translate, route requests, analyze data, model scenarios — making administration dramatically better.
But AI also introduces a danger: The decision can become incomprehensible even to the person exercising the power.
Distinguish Assistance, Consequential Recommendation, and Exercise of Public Power. Safeguards increase as consequence increases.

sections.heading: Digital Due Process
prose: If government uses technology in consequential decisions, affected people need meaningful ability to understand and challenge what happened.
Model/System → Decision → Reason → Human accountability → Appeal.

We retain Stage 4 uncertainty about exactly where every legal state-action boundary falls — don't fake a bright line. But: Government should not gain the power to make decisions nobody can explain merely because software made them faster.

sections.heading: Data rights
prose: Better government needs data. But data concentration creates power.
Collection should connect to legitimate purpose, security, appropriate access, retention rules, auditability, and due process where consequences follow.
No surveillance-policy rabbit hole — the point is institutional design.

sections.heading: Emergency power
prose: Emergencies sometimes require extraordinary speed. But emergency authority tends to persist.
Stage 4 locked: trigger, scope, duration, oversight, sunset, review.
An emergency can justify temporary extraordinary authority. It should not quietly rewrite ordinary government.

sections.heading: Institutional entropy
prose: Institutions drift. Programs accumulate. Rules layer. Temporary offices become permanent. Measures become outdated. Organizations learn to protect themselves.
Government needs mechanisms to ask periodically: Why does this still exist? Is it accomplishing its purpose? Is there a better way?
That's institutional entropy — and renewal.

sections.heading: Measurement can become another form of capture
prose: A government begins measuring success. Good. Then people learn which number determines funding or praise. Soon they optimize the number.
A school can improve a metric without improving education. An agency can close easy cases to improve completion rates. A program can serve easier populations to improve outcomes.
Therefore CC uses panels of measures + countermetrics + qualitative review — not one magic score. Same reason Household Prosperity isn't one number.

sections.heading: The Opposition Test again
prose: Take every new power proposed in Chapters 1–5 — public investment, data, AI, economic development, emergency capacity, planning, measurement.
Would I give this power to my political opponent?
If not: narrow it, constrain it, make it transparent, add appeal, or don't create it. That's constitutional design.

sections.heading: The real enemy isn't government or business
prose: The problem isn't government versus business. The deeper danger is unaccountable concentrated power.
It can exist in government, corporations, monopolies, political machines, institutions, platforms, organizations — even local systems.
Constitutional Capitalism tries to distribute power, create counterweights and preserve meaningful choice.

sections.heading: Evidence informs. Experts administer. Institutions constrain. Citizens govern.
prose: Evidence informs — reality matters more than ideology.
Experts administer — complex systems require competence.
Institutions constrain — nobody gets unlimited discretion.
Citizens govern — technical expertise never becomes sovereignty.

sections.heading: Return to the Rivers household
prose: What does any of this mean to them? They should be able to know where public money went, why a government decision affected them, how to challenge a mistake, who benefited from a public deal, who has authority, what data were used — and ultimately who can be removed from office.
Government belonging to the people isn't a philosophical abstraction. It's a relationship of power.

sections.heading: The closing argument
prose: Constitutional Capitalism does not ask Arkansans to trust government more. Nor does it ask them to trust corporations, experts, algorithms, political parties or wealthy benefactors more. It asks us to build institutions that require less trust because power can be seen, challenged, divided, measured and ultimately returned to the people from whom it came.
Government should be strong enough to protect a free society, capable enough to serve it, and constrained enough that it can never legitimately claim to own it.
Next: you've now seen the pieces. Pass 5.7 names the political-economic philosophy they form — and where it agrees with, borrows from, and rejects the traditions that came before it.
